				<td valign="bottom" style="width:01.10%;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-left:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:2pt double #000000 ;border-right:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;background-color: #CCEEFF;padding:0pt;">
					<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 7pt;">
						<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:7pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
				</td>
				<td valign="bottom" style="width:04.70%;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-left:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:2pt double #000000 ;border-right:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;background-color: #CCEEFF;padding:0pt;">
					<p style="margin:0pt 2.4pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:right;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 7pt;">
						<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:7pt;"> 100.0</font></p>
				</td>
				<td valign="bottom" style="width:01.28%;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-left:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-right:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;background-color: #CCEEFF;padding:0pt;">
					<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 7pt;">
						<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:7pt;">%</font></p>
				</td>
			</tr>
		</table></div>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">We believe that any allocation of the allowance into categories creates an appearance of precision that does not exist. The allocation table should not be interpreted as an indication of the specific amounts, by loan classification, to be charged to the allowance. We believe that the table is a useful device for assessing the adequacy of the allowance as a whole. The allowance is utilized as a single unallocated allowance available for all loans. &nbsp;As part of the overall allowance, the Company maintains an unallocated portion that is intended to capture the inherent risk that certain loans may be assigned an incorrect loan grade.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company determines the level of the unallocated allowance by reference to its migration of historical losses and the percentage of loans identified as incorrectly graded through the loan review process.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The Company recorded a $3.2 million provision for loan losses during 2017 compared to a $2.1 million provision for loan losses reversal during 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;The provision for loan losses in 2017 was primarily a function of loan growth, while the negative provision in 2016 was due to improvement in the credit quality of the loan portfolio, loan loss recoveries and the release of a specific reserve on an impaired credit.&nbsp;&nbsp;Nonperforming assets increased $4.6 million, or 54.6% to $12.9 million at December 31, 2017 from $8.4 million a year earlier.&nbsp;&nbsp;The increase in nonperforming assets was due to nonaccrual loans, which increased but only represent 0.24% of the total loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company had charge-offs of $0.9 million and $7.8 million during 2017 and 2016, respectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company had recoveries of $2.3 million and $2.5 million in 2017 and 2016, respectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;Although the Company continues to record charge-offs, management believes that its credit quality outlook remains favorable and that the Company&#x2019;s allowance for loan and credit losses provides adequate coverage for probable loan and credit losses.&nbsp;&nbsp;The allowance for loan and credit losses to total loans was 1.21% and 1.13% at December 31, 2017 and 2016, respectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;The allowance for loan and credit losses to nonperforming loans was&nbsp;482.4% &nbsp;and 1,010.4% at December 31, 2017 and 2016, respectively.&nbsp; It is possible management may determine a need to increase the allowance for loan and credit losses due to changes in the factors considered by management in evaluating the adequacy of the allowance for loan and credit losses.&nbsp;&nbsp;Such determination could have an adverse effect in the level of future loan and credit loss provisions and the Company&#x2019;s earnings.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Investments</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The investment portfolio is primarily composed of residential MBS explicitly (GNMA) and implicitly (FNMA and FHLMC) backed by the U.S. Government, with the majority of the portfolio either maturing or repricing within one to five years. The portfolio does not include any securities exposed to sub-prime mortgage loans. The investment portfolio also includes single-issuer TPS and corporate debt securities. The corporate debt securities portfolio primarily consists of senior and subordinated debentures issued by the financial services industry.&nbsp; None of the issuing institutions are in default nor have interest payments on the TPS been deferred.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our investment strategies are reviewed in meetings of the ALCO.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The Company views its reciprocal CDARS and ICS accounts as customer-related deposits.&nbsp; The CDARS and ICS programs are provided through a third party and are designed to provide full FDIC insurance on deposit amounts by exchanging or reciprocating larger depository relationships with other member banks. Depositor funds are broken into smaller amounts and placed with other banks that are members of the network. Each member bank issues deposit amounts at a level that the entire deposit is eligible for FDIC insurance. CDARS and ICS are technically brokered deposits; however, the Company considers the reciprocal deposits placed through these programs as core funding due to the customer relationship that generated the transaction and does not report the balances as brokered sources in its internal or external financial reports.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company had balances of $344.9 million and $327.8 million in CDARS and ICS accounts at December 31, 2017 and 2016, respectively. &nbsp;</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Earnings Performance</font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">. Net income for the year ended December 31, 2017 was $32.9 million, a 5.7% decrease from $34.9 million in 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;The decrease in net income was due to a $7.2 million increase in tax expense as a result of the TCJA. The increase to tax expense also reduced the return on average assets and equity.&nbsp;&nbsp;Return on average assets decreased to 0.87% for 2017 compared to 1.02% in 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;Return on average shareholders&#x2019; equity decreased to 10.27% from 12.15% in 2016.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">average shareholders&#x2019; equity also increased in 2016 to 12.15% from 8.77% in 2015.&nbsp;&nbsp;The financial improvement in 2016 was due to an increase in net interest income of $4.4 million and a decrease of $8.5 million in the provision for loan losses in 2016 over 2015.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Earnings per common share on a diluted basis for the year ended December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017,&nbsp;2016 and 2015, &nbsp;was $0.78, $0.84 and $0.62, respectively.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Net Interest Income</font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">. The largest component of our net income is our net interest income. NII is the difference between interest income, principally from loans and investment securities, and interest expense, principally on customer deposits and borrowings. Changes in NII result from changes in volume, net interest spread and net interest margin. Volume refers to the average dollar levels of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities. Net interest spread refers to the difference between the average yield on interest-earning assets and the average cost of interest-bearing liabilities. Net interest margin refers to NII divided by average interest-earning assets and is influenced by the level and relative mix of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The majority of our assets are interest-earning and our liabilities are interest-bearing.&nbsp;&nbsp;Accordingly, changes in interest rates may impact our net interest margin. The FOMC uses the federal funds rate, which is the interest rate used by banks to lend to each other, to influence interest rates and the national economy. Changes in the federal funds rate have a direct correlation to changes in one month Libor and the the prime rate, the underlying indeces for most of the floating-rate loans issued by the Company.&nbsp;&nbsp;The target federal funds rate was held at a range of 0-25 basis points between December 2008 and December 2015.&nbsp;&nbsp;On December 17, 2015, the FOMC increased the target rate to 25-50 basis points, the first increase since June 2006.&nbsp;&nbsp;The target rate was increased another 100 basis points between 2016-2017 and is at a range of 125-150 basis at December 31, 2017.&nbsp;&nbsp;As the Company is asset sensitive, low rates negatively impact the Company&#x2019;s earnings and NIM and the Company benefits as the target rate increases.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The following table presents, for the periods indicated, certain information related to our average asset and liability structure and our average yields on assets and average costs of liabilities. Such yields are derived by dividing income or expense by the average balance of the corresponding assets or liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;NII and NIM are presented on a taxable-equivalent basis to recognize the income tax savings when comparing taxable and tax-exempt assets. &nbsp;The taxable-equivalent NII and NIM in the following table were computed using the applicable state tax rate and a 35.0% federal tax rate.&nbsp;&nbsp;Beginning in 2018, the taxable-equivalent NII and NIM </font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Average interest-earning assets increased $316.4 million to $3.63 billion at December 31, 2017, primarily due to an increase of $252.6 million in the loan portfolio and $74.2 million in the investment portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;Taxable-equivalent net interest income grew $16.0 million due to the growth in the loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;The yield on earning assets increased 11 basis points, from 4.09% to 4.20% in 2017, primarily due to a 12 basis point increase in the yield on the loan portfolio.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Average interest-bearing liabilities increased $143.7 million during 2017 to $2.03 billion.&nbsp;&nbsp;The increase was due to a $106.1 million increase in interest-bearing deposits and a $37.6 million increase in Customer Repurchases and short-term borrowings. The average cost of liabilities was 0.62% in both 2017 and 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;Although the cost of short-term borrowings increased 53 basis points in 2017 due to the increase in the target federal funds rate, the overall cost of deposits remained stable at 13 basis points in both 2017 and 2016.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Average interest-earning assets increased $268.2 million to $3.31 billion at December 31, 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;The loan portfolio increased $275.8 million in 2016, while the investment portfolio declined $15.9 million, the sixth consecutive year the investment portfolio has declined.&nbsp;&nbsp;Taxable-equivalent net interest income grew $6.2 million due to the growth in interest-earning assets, primarily in the loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, net interest income included 366 days in 2016 due to the leap year, compared to 365 days in 2015.&nbsp;&nbsp;The yield on earning assets declined nine basis points, from 4.18% to 4.09% in 2016, primarily due to a lower yield on the loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;In October 2016, the Company entered into two interest-rate swaps to hedge the cash flows on a portion of its LIBOR-based loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;The swaps have a weighted average term of six years and a combined notional value of $100.0 million.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company pays a variable rate based on 1-month LIBOR and receives a weighted average fixed-rate of 1.20%.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Average interest-bearing liabilities increased $123.4 million during 2016 to $1.88 billion.&nbsp;&nbsp;The increase was due to an $83.8 million increase in interest-bearing deposits and a $39.6 million net increase in Customer Repurchases and short/long-term borrowings. The average cost of liabilities increased in 2016, to 0.62%, from 0.55% in 2015.&nbsp;&nbsp;The increase in the yield on interest-bearing liabilities was primarily due to the increase in the target federal funds rate in December 2015, which increased short-term borrowing costs in 2016.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The Company has executed a series of interest-rate swap transactions designated as cash flow hedges. The swaps fix the effective interest rate for payments due on the junior subordinated debentures with the objective of reducing the Company&#x2019;s exposure to adverse changes in cash flows relating to payments on its LIBOR-</font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-style:normal;font-size:10pt;">The Company recorded a loan loss provision of $3.3 million, ($2.1) million, and $6.4 million during 2017, 2016, and 2015, respectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;The increase in the provision for loan losses in 2017 was primarily due to loan growth, an additional allowance segmentation on a pool of investor office loans within the Denver market and an increase in classified loans.&nbsp;&nbsp;Partially offsetting these items were net recoveries of $1.36 million.&nbsp; </font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-style:normal;font-size:10pt;">The decrease in the provision for loan losses in 2016 was primarily due to the reversal of a $2.3 million specific reserve on an impaired credit, recoveries of $2.5 million and a decrease in multi-family lending, a category with a higher reserve allocation.&nbsp;&nbsp;Partially offsetting these items were loan growth and a $6.8 million increase in classified loans in 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-style:italic;">Service Charges</font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Deposit service charges primarily consist of fees earned from our treasury management services. Customers are given the option to pay for these services in cash or by offsetting the fees for these services against an earnings credit that is given for maintaining noninterest-bearing deposits. Fees earned from treasury management services will fluctuate based on the number of customers using the services and from changes in U.S. Treasury rates which are used as a benchmark for the earnings credit rate. Other miscellaneous deposit charges are transactional by nature and may not be consistent period over period.&nbsp;&nbsp;As the earnings credit rate increases, the amount of cash fees paid for service charges decreases.&nbsp;&nbsp;In the fourth quarter of 2016, the Company evaluated and increased the rates assessed for treasury management services which increased 2017 income.</font>

Average AUM was $908.7 million, $831.8 million and $876.0, in 2017, 2016 and 2015, respectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;Revenue from investment&nbsp;&nbsp;advisory income benefits from market appreciation and is negatively impacted from market depreciation.</font>

Selected Financial Data).&nbsp;&nbsp;The efficiency ratio is a measure of the Company&#x2019;s overhead, measuring the percentage of each dollar of income that is paid in operating expenses.&nbsp;&nbsp;In 2017 the Company was successful in improving its operating leverage by growing net interest income while limiting the growth in expenses.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company maintains its goal of reducing the efficiency ratio over the next few years and is committed to exploring cost-reduction strategies.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, assuming no other changes, the TCJA will cause the efficiency ratio to increase in 2018 due to the reduction in taxable-equivalent net interest income discussed above.&nbsp;&nbsp;Further increases in the federal funds target rate by the FOMC would benefit the Company&#x2019;s net interest income and efficiency ratio.&nbsp; </font>

The Company&#x2019;s full-time equivalent employee base at the end of 2017 was 538 compared to 533 in 2016.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Salaries and employee benefits increased $3.6 million or 5.1% during the year ended December 31, 2017.&nbsp;&nbsp;Contributing to the increase in 2017 was a $2.1 million increase in salaries and a $1.4 million increase in bonus expense.&nbsp;&nbsp;Salaries increased due to the annual cost of living and merit increases effective in the second quarter of 2017 and the increase in full-time equivalent employees.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Salaries and employee benefits increased $1.9 million or 2.8% during the year ended December 31, 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;Contributing to the increase in 2016 was a $0.9 million increase in salaries and commission expense, $0.6 million increase in 401(k) matching expense and a $0.5 million increase in insurance benefits.&nbsp;&nbsp;Salaries were also impacted by the annual cost of living and merit increases effective in the second quarter of 2016, offset by a decrease in severance expense in 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company has a 401(k) matching program that is based on the overall profitability of the Company.&nbsp;&nbsp;Based on the Company&#x2019;s financial performance in 2016, an additional match of $0.5 million was made in 2016 that was not made in 2015.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company is partially self-insured on its medical and dental programs.&nbsp;&nbsp;Insurance benefits will vary based on participant claims.&nbsp;&nbsp;In 2016, the Company&#x2019;s participants experienced several large claims that increased our insurance expense.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Included in salaries and employee benefits is expense related to share-based compensation used to retain existing employees and to recruit new employees.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company expects to continue using share-based compensation in the future as it is considered an important part of overall compensation.&nbsp;&nbsp;Costs associated with the plan are influenced by the number of participants in the Company&#x2019;s stock bonus pool and the proportion of incentive compensation paid in cash versus stock.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-style:italic;">Occupancy Expenses, Premises and Equipment</font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Occupancy expenses consist primarily of rent, utilities, property taxes, insurance, depreciation and information systems maintenance.&nbsp;&nbsp;Occupancy costs decreased $0.3 million or 2.0% during the year ended December 31, 2017 compared to 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;In January 2016, the Company signed a new lease agreement for its principal executive offices and recognized seven months of expense related to the lease in 2016, in addition to a full year of expense on the former principal executive office lease that terminated on December 31, 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;The transition cost of maintaining leases on two locations did not reocurr in 2017.&nbsp;&nbsp;Occupancy costs increased $1.9 million or 14.4% during the year ended December 31, 2016 compared to 2015.&nbsp;&nbsp;The increase in 2016 was due to the cost of maintaining leases on two locations for part of 2016.&nbsp; </font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The Commercial Banking segment reported net income of $39.0 million and $40.2 million during 2017 and 2016, respectively. Volume increases in our interest earning assets and an increase in yield were the primary reasons for the increase in net interest income.&nbsp;&nbsp;Average loans increased $252.6 million and the yield on interest-earning assets increased 11 basis points in 2017.&nbsp;&nbsp;The growth in the loan portfolio also resulted in an increase to our provision for loan losses, which increased $5.2 million in 2017 over 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;Noninterest expense decreased $4.0 million in 2017 compared to 2016, partially due to a decline in occupancy costs associated with the Company&#x2019;s move to a new headquarters location in 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, certain centralized expenses included in the Commercial Banking segment in 2016 were moved to the Corporate Support segment in 2017.&nbsp;&nbsp;The provision for income taxes increased $9.3 million in 2017 compared to 2016 due to higher pre-tax income and the impact of the TCJA.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The Commercial Banking segment reported net income of $40.2 million and $29.8 million during 2016 and 2015, respectively. Volume increases in our interest earning assets was the primary reason for the increase in net interest income.&nbsp;&nbsp;Average loans were $275.8 million higher in 2016 than in 2015, which muted the effect of lower yields on interest-earning assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;Asset quality improvements and recoveries on charged-off loans resulted in a loan loss provision reversal of $1.8 million.&nbsp;&nbsp;Noninterest income grew in 2016, primarily due to $1.2 million in fees generated from the sale of interest rate swaps.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">During the first quarter of 2015, the Company ceased operations of GMB, a provider of investment banking services that was a component of the Fee-Based Lines segment.&nbsp;&nbsp;The decision was based in part by&nbsp;&nbsp;increasing regulatory compliance costs related to maintaining GMB&#x2019;s broker-dealer license and earnings volatility which was highly dependent on deal volume.&nbsp;&nbsp;Results for GMB for 2015 have been reclassified as discontinued operations.&nbsp;&nbsp;See Note 2 &#x2013; Discontinued Operations for additional discussion.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">Net loss in the Fee-Based Lines segment decreased $0.8 million in 2017 compared to 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;An increase in noninterest income of $1.1 million, while noninterest expense remained relatively flat, was the primary reason for the improvement.&nbsp;&nbsp;The increase in tax expense from the TCJA also impacted the Fee-Based Lines, increasing tax expense by $0.5 million.&nbsp;&nbsp;Absent the increase in tax expense from the TCJA,&nbsp;&nbsp;the segment would have reported a positive net income.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">Net loss in the Fee-Based Lines segment increased $0.7 million in 2016 compared to 2015.&nbsp;&nbsp;Lower investment advisory and insurance revenue coupled with higher salary and benefit costs contributed to the net loss in 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At December 31, 2016, AUM decreased $14.7 million during 2016 to $844.5 million from $859.2 million at the end of 2015.&nbsp;&nbsp;Average AUM in 2016 was $831.8 million compared to $876.0 million in 2015.&nbsp;&nbsp;Noninterest expense in the segment is predominately compensation-related, which is primarily variable and directly related to revenue.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, as the Company invests in new production staff, compensation as a percentage of revenue for those employees is higher in the earlier years until those new producers build a revenue base.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">For the year ended December 31, 2017, the segment reported a net loss of $5.7 million, an increase of $1.6 million from 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;Lower noninterest income was due to the earnings on the Company&#x2019;s investments in mezzanine funds, which decreased in 2017 compared to 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;Continued investment in the operational redesign of the Company&#x2019;s credit process, business intelligence and other consulting services resulted in an increase in noninterest expense during 2017. </font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">The segment reported a net loss of $4.1 million in 2016 compared to a net loss of $3.2 million in the prior year.&nbsp;&nbsp;Lower net interest income was the result of additional interest expense of $1.7 million in 2016 relating to the Notes and lower interest income due to a prior-year recapture of $1.0 million of interest income on problem loan resolutions.&nbsp;&nbsp;Higher salary, health insurance, facility rents and service contract costs resulted in an increase in noninterest expense during 2016. </font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The provision for loan losses relates to a portfolio of loans purchased by the Parent from the Bank. This portfolio has steadily decreased since the 2009 purchase due to loan repayments and collateral sales.&nbsp;&nbsp;The declining balance of the portfolio and the overall asset quality improvement has contributed to the trend of declining provision for loan losses.&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 9pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;">Liquidity and Capital Resources</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">Liquidity refers to the Company&#x2019;s ability to generate adequate amounts of cash to meet financial obligations to its customers and shareholders in order to fund loans, to respond to deposit outflows and to cover operating expenses.&nbsp;&nbsp;Maintaining a level of liquid funds through asset/liability management seeks to ensure that these needs are met at a reasonable cost.&nbsp;&nbsp;Liquidity is essential to compensate for fluctuations in the balance sheet and provide funds for growth and normal operating expenditures.&nbsp;&nbsp;Sources of funds include customer deposits, scheduled amortization of loans, loan prepayments, scheduled maturities and calls of investments and prepayments from mortgage-backed securities.&nbsp;&nbsp;Liquidity needs may also be met by deposit growth, converting assets into cash, raising funds in the brokered CD market or borrowing using lines of credit with correspondent banks, the FHLB or the FRB.&nbsp;&nbsp;Longer-term liquidity needs may be met by selling securities available for sale or raising additional capital.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">Liquidity management is the process by which the Company manages the continuing flow of funds necessary to meet its financial commitments on a timely basis and at a reasonable cost. The objective of liquidity management is to ensure the Company has the ability to satisfy the cash flow requirements of depositors and borrowers and to allow us to sustain our operations.&nbsp;&nbsp;These funding commitments include withdrawals by depositors, credit commitments to borrowers, shareholder dividends, debt payments, expenses of our operations and capital expenditures.&nbsp;&nbsp;Liquidity is monitored and closely managed by ALCO, a group of senior officers from the lending, deposit gathering, finance and treasury areas.&nbsp;&nbsp;ALCO&#x2019;s primary responsibilities are to ensure the necessary level of funds are available for normal operations as well as maintain a contingency funding policy to ensure that liquidity stress events are quickly identified and management plans are in place to respond.&nbsp;&nbsp;This is accomplished through the use of policies which establish limits and require measurements to monitor liquidity trends, including management reporting that identifies the amounts and costs of all available funding sources.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">The Company's current liquidity position is expected to be more than adequate to fund expected asset growth.&nbsp;&nbsp;Historically, our primary source of funds has been customer deposits.&nbsp;&nbsp;Scheduled loan repayments are a relatively stable source of funds, while deposit inflows and unscheduled loan prepayments &#x2013; which are influenced by fluctuations in the general level of interest rates, returns available on other investments, competition, economic conditions, and other factors &#x2013; are less predictable.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">53</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#Toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;">Table of Contents</a></font>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">Liquidity from asset categories is provided through cash and interest-bearing deposits with other banks, which totaled $80.2 million at December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017, compared to $96.1 million at December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additional asset liquidity sources include principal and interest payments from securities in the Company&#x2019;s investment portfolio and loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;Liability liquidity sources include attracting deposits at competitive rates and maintaining wholesale borrowing (short-term borrowings and brokered CDs) credit relationships.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">The Company&#x2019;s loan to core deposit ratio increased to 97.5% at December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017, from 96.8% at December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;At December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017 and 2016, the Company had $77.6 million and $106.2 million in outstanding wholesale borrowings, respectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;Average wholesale borrowings were $108.7 million and $84.8 million during the years ended December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017 and 2016.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">The Company uses various forms of short-term borrowings for cash management and liquidity purposes, regularly accessing its federal funds and FHLB lines to manage its daily cash position. At December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017, the Bank has approved federal funds purchase lines with eight correspondent banks with an aggregate credit line of $180.0 million.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank also has a line of credit from the FHLB that is limited by the amount of eligible collateral available to secure it and the Company&#x2019;s investment in FHLB stock.&nbsp;&nbsp;Borrowings under the FHLB line are required to be secured by unpledged securities and qualifying loans. Borrowings may also be used on a longer-term basis to support expanded lending activities and to match the maturity or repricing intervals of assets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">Available funding through correspondent lines and the FHLB at December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017, totaled $709.2 million or 19.2% of the Company&#x2019;s earning assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;Available funding consisted of &nbsp;$180.0 million of federal fund lines and $529.2 million in secured FHLB borrowing capacity.&nbsp;&nbsp;Access to funding through correspondent lines is dependent upon the cash position of the correspondent banks and there may be times when certain lines are not available.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, certain lines require a one day rest period after a specified number of consecutive days of accessing the lines. The Company believes it has sufficient borrowing capacity and diversity in correspondent banks to meet its needs.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">At the holding company level, our primary sources of funds are dividends paid from the Bank and fee-based subsidiaries, management fees assessed to the Bank and the Fee-Based Lines, proceeds from the issuance of common stock, and other capital markets activity.&nbsp;&nbsp;The main use of this liquidity is the quarterly payment of dividends on our common stock, quarterly interest payments on the subordinated debentures and notes payable, payments for mergers and acquisitions activity, and payments for the salaries and benefits for the employees of the holding company.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;color:#000000;font-family:Arial Unicode MS;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The Company also maintains a revolving line of credit for an aggregate amount of up to $20.0 million, all of which was available at December 31,&nbsp;2017.&nbsp;&nbsp;The line of credit has a one year term and matures in May 2018.&nbsp;&nbsp;Funds drawn will be used for general corporate purposes and backup liquidity.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial Unicode MS;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">The approval of the Colorado State Banking Board is required prior to the declaration of any dividend by the Bank if the total of all dividends declared by the Bank in any calendar year exceeds the total of its net profits for that year combined with the retained net profits for the preceding two years.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act of 1991 provides that the Bank cannot pay a dividend if it will cause the Bank to be &#x201C;undercapitalized.&#x201D;&nbsp;&nbsp;At December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017, the Bank was not otherwise restricted in its ability to pay dividends to the holding company.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#x2019;s ability to pay dividends on its common stock depends upon the availability of dividends from the Bank, earnings from its Fee-Based Lines, and upon the Company&#x2019;s compliance with the capital adequacy guidelines of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors (see Note 17 &#x2013; Regulatory Matters).&nbsp;&nbsp;The holding company has a liquidity policy that requires the maintenance of at least 18 months of liquidity on the balance sheet based on projected cash usages, exclusive of dividends from the Bank.&nbsp;&nbsp;At December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017, the Company had a liquidity position that exceeds the policy limit, and we believe the Company has the ability to continue paying dividends.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">We anticipate that our cash and cash equivalents, expected cash flows from continuing operations together with alternative sources of funding are sufficient to meet our anticipated cash requirements for working capital, loan originations, capital expenditures and other obligations for at least the next 12&nbsp;months.&nbsp;&nbsp;We continually monitor existing and alternative financing sources to support our capital and liquidity needs, including but not limited to, debt issuance, common stock issuance and deposit funding sources.&nbsp;&nbsp;Based on our current financial condition and our results of operations, we believe the Company will be able to sustain its ability to raise adequate capital through one or more of these financing sources.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">We are subject to minimum risk-based capital limitations as set forth by federal banking regulations at both the consolidated Company level and the Bank level. Under the risk-based capital guidelines, different categories of assets, including certain off-balance sheet items, such as loan commitments in excess of one year and letters of credit, are assigned different risk weights, based generally on the perceived credit risk of the asset. These risk weights are multiplied by corresponding asset balances to determine a &#x201C;risk-weighted&#x201D; asset base. For purposes of the risk-based capital guidelines, total capital is defined as the sum of &#x201C;Common Equity Tier 1,&#x201D; &#x201C;Additional Tier 1&#x201D; and &#x201C;Tier 2&#x201D; capital elements. Common Equity Tier 1 consists of common stock, related surplus and retained earnings.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additional Tier 1 capital includes, with certain restrictions, noncumulative perpetual preferred stock, certain grandfathered regulatory capital instruments and minority interests in consolidated subsidiaries. Tier 2 capital includes, with certain limitations, perpetual preferred stock not included in Tier 1 capital, subordinated debt, certain maturing capital instruments, and the allowance for loan and credit losses.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Courier New;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Beginning in 2016, the CCB requirement became effective for banking organizations.&nbsp;&nbsp;The CCB is designed to establish a capital range above minimum requirements to insulate banks from periods of stress and discourage unacceptable practices that may shift certain risks from an organization&#x2019;s shareholders to its depositors.&nbsp;&nbsp;When the capital buffer is breached, an organization&#x2019;s ability to pay dividends, execute share repurchases and make discretionary bonus payments may be limited to varying degrees depending on the severity of the breach.&nbsp;&nbsp;When fully phased-in in 2019, the CCB adds a 2.5% capital requirement above existing regulatory minimum ratios.&nbsp;&nbsp;At December &nbsp;31, 2017, the Bank and Holding Company maintained capital buffers in excess of the fully phased-in requirements and were not subject to additional constraints on distributions, share repurchases or discretionary bonus payments beyond existing limits.&nbsp;&nbsp;At December &nbsp;31, 2017, the Bank was well-capitalized with all capital ratios exceeding the well-capitalized requirement.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">See Note 17 &#x2013; Regulatory Matters for additional capital ratio disclosure.&nbsp;&nbsp;In order to comply with the regulatory capital constraints, the Company and its Board of Directors constantly monitor the capital level and its anticipated needs based on the Company&#x2019;s growth. The Company has identified sources of additional capital that could be used if needed, and monitors the costs and benefits of these sources, which include both the public and private markets.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">56</font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#Toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;">Table of Contents</a></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The Company is party to financial instruments with off-balance sheet risk in the normal course of business to meet the liquidity, credit enhancement and financing needs of its customers. These financial instruments include legally binding commitments to extend credit and standby letters of credit and involve, to varying degrees, elements of credit and interest rate risk in excess of the amount recognized on the balance sheet. Credit risk is the principal risk associated with these instruments. The contractual amounts of these instruments represent the amount of credit risk should the instruments be fully drawn upon and the customer defaults. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">To control the credit risk associated with entering into commitments and issuing letters of credit, the Company uses the same credit quality, collateral policies and monitoring controls in making commitments and letters of credit as it does with its lending activities. The Company evaluates each customer&#x2019;s creditworthiness on a case-by-case basis. The amount of collateral obtained, if deemed necessary by the Company upon extension of credit, is based on management&#x2019;s credit evaluation. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Legally binding commitments to extend credit are agreements to lend to a customer as long as there is no violation of any condition established in the contract. Commitments generally have fixed expiration dates or other termination clauses and may require payment of a fee. Since many of the commitments may expire without being drawn upon, the total commitment amounts do not necessarily represent future cash requirements. Standby letters of credit obligate the Company to meet certain financial obligations of its customers if, under the contractual terms of the agreement, the customers are unable to do so. The financial standby letters of credit issued by the Company are irrevocable. Payment is only guaranteed under these letters of credit upon the borrower&#x2019;s failure to perform its obligations to the beneficiary. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Approximately $52.8 million of total commitments at December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017 represent commitments to extend credit at fixed-rates of interest, which exposes the Company to some degree of interest rate risk.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The Company has also entered into interest-rate swap agreements under which it is required to either receive or pay cash to a counterparty depending on changes in interest rates. The interest-rate swaps are carried at their fair value on the consolidated balance sheet with the fair value representing the net present value of expected future cash receipts or payments based on market interest rates at the balance sheet date. Interest-rate swaps recorded on the consolidated balance sheet at December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017, do not represent amounts that will ultimately be received or paid under the contract and are therefore excluded from the table above.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 9pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;">Effects of Inflation and Changing Prices</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The primary impact of inflation on our operations is increased operating costs. Unlike most retail or manufacturing companies, virtually all of the assets and liabilities of a financial institution such as the Company are monetary in nature. As a result, the impact of interest rates on a financial institution's performance is generally greater than the impact of inflation. Although interest rates do not necessarily move in the same direction, or to the same extent, as the prices of goods and services, increases in inflation generally have resulted in increased interest rates. Over short periods of time, interest rates may not move in the same direction, or at the same magnitude, as inflation.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 9pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;">Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative<a name="Item7AQuantitativeandQualitative_224531"></a> Disclosures About Market Risk</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;">Asset/Liability Management</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;color:#3C5C54;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Asset/liability management is concerned with the timing and magnitude of repricing assets compared to liabilities. It is our objective to generate stable growth in net interest income and to attempt to control risks associated with interest rate movements. In general, our strategy is to reduce the impact of changes in interest rates on net interest income by maintaining a favorable match between the maturities or repricing dates of our interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities. Interest sensitivity changes during the year through changes in the mix of assets and liabilities. Our asset and liability management strategy is formulated and monitored by ALCO, in accordance with policies approved by the Board of Directors of the Bank. This </font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">57</font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#Toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;">Table of Contents</a></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">committee meets regularly to review, among other things, the sensitivity of our assets and liabilities to interest rate changes, the book and market values of assets and liabilities, unrealized gains and losses, purchase and sale activity, and maturities of investments and borrowings.&nbsp; ALCO also approves and establishes pricing and funding decisions with respect to our overall asset and liability composition. The committee reviews our liquidity, cash flow flexibility, maturities of investments, deposits and borrowings, deposit activity, current market conditions, and general levels of interest rates. To effectively measure and manage interest rate risk, we use simulation analysis to determine the impact&nbsp;of changes in interest rates on net interest income under various interest rate scenarios. From these simulations, interest rate risk is quantified and appropriate strategies are developed and implemented.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">The following table presents an analysis of the interest rate sensitivity inherent in our net interest income (NII) and economic value of equity (EVE). 		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">There are two NII simulations presented, the first being an instantaneous or immediate shock to the yield curve in a parallel fashion down 100 basis points and up 100 and 200 basis points and and the second being a 12 month ramp of the yield curve in a parallel fashion down 100 basis points and up 100 and 200 basis points.&nbsp;&nbsp;Consequently, the sensitivity in the year 1 ramped simulation is less than the immediate simulation since the rate movements are applies incrementally over the course of the first year.&nbsp;&nbsp;The NII sensitivity analysis presented includes assumptions that (i) the yield curve used throughout the NII simulation is static as opposed to using implied forward rates; (ii) loan repricing spreads are based on actual originations of new loans over the past year; (iii) deposit average lives and repricing betas are based on a multi-year historical study; (iv) loan prepayment speeds are approximations; and (v) no balance sheet growth is assumed.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, we do assume that a portion of our DDA accounts with balances exceeding $250,000 are &#x201C;surge&#x201D; balances, or balances that are at risk of leaving the bank and/or moving into more expensive deposit types if interest rates return to higher historical averages.&nbsp;&nbsp;Further, the analysis does not contemplate any actions that we might undertake in response to changes in market interest rates. Accordingly, this analysis is not intended to and does not provide a precise forecast of the effect actual changes in market rates will have on us.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Our results of operations depend significantly on net interest income. Like most financial institutions, our interest income and cost of funds are affected by general economic conditions and by competition in the marketplace. Rising and falling interest rate environments can have various impacts on net interest income, depending on the interest rate profile (i.e., the difference between the repricing of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities), the relative changes in interest rates that occur when various assets and liabilities reprice, unscheduled repayments of loans and investments, early withdrawals of deposits, and other factors. As a general rule, banks with positive interest rate gaps are more likely to be susceptible to declines in net interest income in periods of falling interest rates, while banks with negative interest rate gaps are more likely to experience declines in net interest income in periods of rising interest rates. At December 31, 2017, our cumulative interest rate gap was a positive 43.2%. Therefore, assuming no change in our gap position, a rise in interest rates is likely to result in increased net interest income, while a decline in interest rates is likely to result in decreased net interest income. This is a point-in-time position that is continually changing and is not indicative of our position at any other time. While the gap position is a useful tool in measuring interest rate risk and contributes toward effective asset and liability management, shortcomings are inherent in gap </font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">58</font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#Toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;">Table of Contents</a></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">analysis since certain assets and liabilities may not move proportionally as interest rates change. Consequently, in addition to gap analysis, we use the simulation model discussed above to test the interest rate sensitivity of net interest income and the balance sheet</font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:8pt;">. &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 8pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:8pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">impact of interest rate fluctuations on our net interest margin. Interest-rate swaps involve the exchange of fixed-rate and variable-rate interest payment obligations without the exchange of the underlying notional amounts.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Under the interest-rate swap agreements, we receive a fixed-rate and pay a variable-rate based on LIBOR. The swaps qualify as cash flow hedges under ASC Topic 815, </font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-style:italic;">Derivatives and Hedging </font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">(ASC 815), and are designated as hedges of the variability of cash flows we received from certain of our LIBOR-based loans. In accordance with ASC 815, these swap agreements are measured at fair value and reported as assets or liabilities on the consolidated balance sheets. The portion of the change in the fair value of the swaps that is deemed effective in hedging the cash flows of the designated assets is recorded in AOCI, net of tax effects, and reclassified to interest income when such cash flows occur in the future. Any ineffectiveness resulting from the hedges is recorded as a gain or loss in the consolidated statements of income as a part of noninterest income.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;">Information on outstanding interest rate swaps at December&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2017 is as follows:</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-style:normal;font-size:10pt;">Since 2009, the Company has managed a series of interest-rate swap transactions designated as cash flow hedges.&nbsp;&nbsp;The intent of the transactions was to fix the effective interest rate of payments due on its junior subordinated debentures with the objective of reducing the Company&#x2019;s exposure to adverse changes in cash flows relating to payments on its LIBOR-based floating-rate debt.&nbsp;&nbsp;The swap agreements in effect at December 31, 2017, have a total notional value of $70.0 million, fix the interest rates between 4.99% and 5.99% and mature over varying lengths of time from two to six years.</font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-style:normal;font-size:10pt;">The Company has initiated certain interest-rate swap transactions designated as fair value hedges under ASC 815.&nbsp;&nbsp;The objective of these transactions is to exchange interest payments received on fixed-rate loans for variable-rate payments.&nbsp;&nbsp;At December 31, 2017, the notional value of these swaps was $59.2 million.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-style:normal;font-size:10pt;">During the years ended December 31, 2017, 2016 and 2015, &nbsp;net interest income decreased $1.4 million, $2.1 million and $2.0 million, respectively, from settlement of the interest-rate swaps.</font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-style:normal;font-size:10pt;">The Company has initiated foreign exchange forward contracts to mitigate exposure to foreign exchange rate risk on foreign currency holdings.&nbsp;&nbsp;Foreign currencies held include the British pound; &nbsp;Euro; &nbsp;Swiss franc; &nbsp;Mexican peso; &nbsp;Japanese yen; &nbsp;and Australian, New Zealand and Canadian dollars.&nbsp;&nbsp;At December 31, 2017, the aggregate notional value of the foreign currency forwards was $4.8 million and all contracts settle within three months or less of date of this report.&nbsp;&nbsp;The effect of foreign currency forwards on noninterest income was immaterial for the years ended December 31, 2017, 2016 and 2015.&nbsp; </font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;">Item 9A. Controls and Procedure<a name="Item9AControlsandProcedures_938591"></a>s</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;display:inline;font-style:normal;font-size:10pt;">Disclosure Controls and Procedures</font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:normal;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;display:inline;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;font-size:10pt;">The Company carried out an evaluation, under the supervision and with the participation of the Company&#x2019;s management, including the Company&#x2019;s CEO and the Company&#x2019;s CFO, of the effectiveness of the design and operation of the Company&#x2019;s disclosure controls and procedures at the end of the period covered by this report pursuant to Exchange Act Rule 13a-15. Based upon that evaluation, the Company&#x2019;s CEO and CFO concluded the Company&#x2019;s disclosure controls and procedures are effective in ensuring that information relating to the Company, including its consolidated subsidiaries, required to be disclosed in reports that it files under the Exchange Act is (1) recorded, processed, summarized and reported within the time periods specified in the SEC&#x2019;s rules and forms; &nbsp;and (2) accumulated and communicated to our management, including our CEO and CFO, as appropriate to allow timely decisions regarding required disclosure.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">Management&#x2019;s Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">Management of CoBiz Financial Inc., together with its consolidated subsidiaries (the Company), is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting. The Company&#x2019;s internal control over financial reporting is a process designed under the supervision of the Company&#x2019;s Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of the Company&#x2019;s financial statements for external reporting purposes in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">As of December 31, 2017, management assessed the effectiveness of the Company&#x2019;s internal control over financial reporting based on the framework established in the </font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">2013</font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Internal Control &#x2014; Integrated Framework </font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:10pt;">issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO).&nbsp;&nbsp;Based on this assessment, management has determined that the Company&#x2019;s internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2017, is effective.</font>
		</p>
